title: Pauri 38, sound: jat paahaaraa
last: SACH KHAND — HARD AS STEEL TO TELL.

lines: A SMALL FURNACE, A LITTLE ANVIL.
cards: An old Punjabi bazaar, and down one side, a goldsmiths' lane. Tiny shops, open to the street.
In each, someone sits cross-legged on the floor beside a small furnace, blowing on the coals through a pipe until they glow orange.
A little anvil, a row of hammers, a pair of tongs, and the steady tap, tap, tap of metal being coaxed into shape. The work is slow. Hurry it, and the gold cracks.
Guru Nanak's hearers would have known shops like these the way you know a coffee shop. In the last pauri of the Japji, he walks you into one.

teach.b: Pauri 38 opens: jat paahaaraa dheeraj suniaar. Four words, each a piece of the workshop. Jat: self-restraint, holding yourself in check.
Paahaaraa: the smith's furnace, the forge. Let restraint be the furnace.

Dheeraj: patience, steadiness; you'll hear it in Punjabi and Hindi today, when someone tells you to keep calm and wait. Suniaar: the goldsmith; in Punjab a jeweler is still called a sunaar. Let patience be the goldsmith.
Now the rhythm. Jat, one short hit. Paahaaraa, long and rolling, like breath on the coals.
Dheeraj, firm. Suniaar, opening out at the end.
A strike, a long breath, a strike, a long breath, like the work itself. Then the next line keeps building the shop: aharan mat, ved hatheeaar.
Aharan: the anvil. Mat: understanding, good sense. Ved: here, knowledge.
Hatheeaar: tools. Let understanding be the anvil and knowledge the tools. The whole Japji began with Guru Nanak saying that thinking a hundred thousand times won't get you there.
Now, at the very end, he gives you a place to work: not a temple of thought but a workshop of patience. Tomorrow, what gets made in it.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 38, the last stanza before the closing salok, uses the tools of a goldsmith's workshop, furnace, anvil and crucible, as a picture of the disciplined life.

o: a weaver who spins thread on a loom
a blacksmith who forges iron tools
a goldsmith, who works gold by hand

games.q: the sound of Pauri 38 — tap the pairs.

s: Pauri 38 is the last pauri of the Japji
after it comes only the closing salok.
suniaar is an old word no one uses anymore
in Punjab a jeweler is still called a sunaar.
in Pauri 38, the goldsmith is patience

games.q: you walk into the workshop of Pauri 38. who is the goldsmith?
games.why: dheeraj suniaar: patience is the goldsmith. restraint is the furnace, and understanding the anvil.

practice: Say the first line aloud, slowly, three times: jat paahaaraa dheeraj suniaar, with jat short like a tap on metal and paahaaraa long like a slow breath on coals; then add aharan mat, ved hatheeaar, once.
Afterward, breathe like a goldsmith working the fire: a slow, steady breath out, as if gently blowing on coals, and a quiet breath in, no rushing.

wordCard.voice: Suniaar, the goldsmith. The last pauri of the Japji opens in a goldsmith's shop: restraint is the furnace, patience the goldsmith, understanding the anvil.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 38: restraint the furnace, patience the goldsmith.

carryVoice: Your line: jat paahaaraa, restraint is the furnace. In this shop, patience does the work. Until tomorrow.
